questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: data treated and managed with the same ownership, valuation, and maintenance discipline as a financial or physical asset is called a ________.
questions.explain: Treating data as an asset means it has an identifiable owner, a measurable value and cost of loss, active maintenance, and a role in real business decisions — the four properties most organizational data still fails to meet in practice.

questions.prompt: Which statement below correctly distinguishes data governance, data management, and data quality, per this course's framing?
options: Governance sets the rules (who decides, what's the policy); management is the technical and operational work of acquiring, storing, and processing data; quality is a measurable outcome of how accurate and complete the data actually is.

Governance sets the rules (who decides, what's the policy); management is a measurable outcome of how accurate the data is; quality is the technical and operational work of storing and processing data.

Data management sits at the center of DAMA-DMBOK's wheel, with governance as just one of the ten surrounding knowledge areas, arranged as an equal spoke alongside data quality, metadata, and every other discipline the framework covers.
Data quality is simply a synonym for data governance, used interchangeably in most organizations.
Data governance is the exclusive responsibility of the IT department, while management and quality are purely business responsibilities.
Data management determines who is accountable for a domain, while governance implements the technical storage and pipelines.
questions.explain: Governance is the rulebook (who decides, what's the policy), management is the operation (the day-to-day technical and operational work), and quality is the scorecard (a measurable outcome). DAMA-DMBOK places governance at the center of its wheel precisely because it supplies the authority and consistency the other ten knowledge areas, including quality, depend on.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps the correct first clause about governance word for word, which is what makes it tempting — but it swaps management's and quality's actual definitions with each other. Management is the operational day-to-day work, not a measurable outcome; quality is the measurable outcome, not operational work. That swap is the one meaningful detail that makes B wrong.

questions.prompt: Select every one of the four properties this course says a real asset has — properties most organizational data fails to meet.
options: Ownership — an identifiable, accountable owner
Measurable value, including the cost of losing it
Active maintenance rather than being created once and left to decay
Accounted for explicitly when business decisions get made
Physical form — it must be tangible to count as a real asset
Universal value — it must be equally valuable in every possible use case
questions.explain: A real asset has an identifiable owner, a measurable value and cost of loss, active maintenance, and a real role in decision-making. Data doesn't need physical form to count, and its value is explicitly contextual — the same dataset can be nearly worthless in one use case and critical in another.

questions.prompt: Match each governance driver to its correct description, per this course.
right: Funded to avoid legal and regulatory consequences, such as GDPR or HIPAA penalties
Funded to make data something people believe and use without double-checking it against a shadow spreadsheet
Funded to accelerate business outcomes — faster decisions, workable AI initiatives — not just to reduce risk
questions.explain: Compliance is the easiest driver to fund because the cost of ignoring it is explicit and legal. Trust is harder to put a dollar figure on but often sustains a program after a compliance deadline passes. Value reframes governance as an enabler rather than a brake on the business.

questions.prompt: This course cites Gartner's estimate that poor data quality costs organizations an average of $12.9 million per year, then calls that figure "best treated as a floor." Why?
options: Most of the real costs — like a lost renewal recorded only as churn, with no link back to the billing error that caused it — never get attributed back to the data problem that caused them, so the true cost is almost always higher than what gets measured
Because Gartner's methodology deliberately underestimates costs by exactly half, as a conservative convention
Because the figure only applies to healthcare organizations, and every other industry's true cost is higher
Because the figure was calculated before AI existed, and is therefore automatically out of date
questions.explain: Most costs of poor data are never attributed back to their root cause — a sales team that lost a renewal to a billing error records that loss as churn, with no link back to the broken record that caused it. That attribution gap is exactly why the cited figure is best treated as a floor, not a ceiling.

questions.prompt: A company buys a data catalog, calls the purchase itself "doing governance," and skips the harder work of actually defining ownership, policy, and decision rights the tool was supposed to support. Which common governance failure pattern is this?
options: Tool-first thinking
No executive sponsorship
No clear decision rights
Governance disconnected from business value
questions.explain: Tool-first thinking is mistaking the purchase of a data catalog, MDM platform, or quality tool for the completion of governance work itself — the early warning sign is a live tool with dashboards, but nobody who can say who's accountable when the dashboard shows a problem.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: DAMA International's diagram placing data governance at the center of ten surrounding data management knowledge areas is known as the ________.
questions.explain: The DAMA Wheel places governance at the hub, with the other ten knowledge areas (data architecture, data quality, metadata management, and so on) arranged as spokes around it — because none of those ten can be done well without governance supplying decision rights, accountability, and policy.

questions.prompt: Match each named governance framework to what it's actually built to solve, per this course.
right: A maturity-benchmarking framework from the EDM Council, producing a structured maturity profile and roadmap
ISACA's IT governance framework, with data governance as one component inside a larger scope
An international standard framing data governance as a board-level responsibility, not an operational IT concern
questions.explain: DCAM is built for maturity benchmarking, COBIT is built for IT governance with data governance as part of its scope, and ISO/IEC 38505 is built for board-level accountability — three different pieces of the puzzle, often combined rather than chosen exclusively.

questions.prompt: An organization runs a formal maturity assessment, reports a score upward to leadership, and files it away with no attached action plan or roadmap. Per this course, what is this called?
options: Governance theater — a maturity score with no attached action plan is a vanity metric, not governance work
A readiness assessment, correctly executed
Federated computational governance
A completed DCAM certification
questions.explain: A maturity assessment is only useful if it identifies specific gaps and feeds directly into a roadmap. A maturity model that just produces a number with no attached action plan is governance theater, not governance work.

questions.prompt: Select every one of the four core questions this course says every operating model has to answer.
options: Where do decisions get made?
Who holds the authority?
How does policy get enforced across the organization?
How does the model scale as the organization grows?
Which specific vendor's data catalog software will be purchased?
What is the exact dollar budget for next year's governance conference travel?
questions.explain: Every real operating model answers where decisions get made, who holds the authority, how policy gets enforced, and how the model scales. A specific vendor choice or a travel budget line are implementation details, not the structural questions an operating model itself has to answer.

questions.prompt: A mid-size healthcare company has three distinct business units (a hospital network, a telehealth platform, a billing subsidiary), all touching HIPAA-regulated patient data, low current governance maturity, and a new CDO with real executive backing. Per this course's five-question framework, what does this point to?
options: Start federated, but scope the centrally-governed piece narrowly to patient-data compliance first, expanding central scope only as maturity grows
A fully centralized model from day one, since regulated data always requires full centralization immediately
A fully decentralized model, since three distinct business units automatically rules out any central coordination
No operating model is needed yet, since maturity is too low to support any model at all
questions.explain: Three distinct business units lean federated; the shared HIPAA exposure is a strong cross-cutting consistency need reinforcing federated with compliance centrally governed; low maturity argues for a staged rollout rather than full federation on day one; and real sponsorship makes centrally-enforced standards actually enforceable. The framework points to starting federated, scoped narrowly, and expanding over time.

questions.prompt: Put the five levels of the Gartner maturity structure referenced in this course in order, from least to most mature.
questions.explain: The structure runs from Aware (knowing governance matters) through Reactive (responding to problems as they arise), Proactive, Managed, up to Optimized — fully measured and continuously improving. Most organizations cluster in the lower-middle levels, not the top.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in RACI, the letter that means "owns the outcome and has final sign-off authority," with exactly one per task, is ________.
questions.explain: Accountable (A) owns the outcome and has final sign-off — there should be exactly one A per task. A task with more than one A hasn't clarified responsibility, it's written down the exact ambiguity governance exists to prevent.

questions.prompt: Which statement below correctly distinguishes a data owner, a data steward, and a data custodian, per DAMA-DMBOK as this course applies it?
options: The owner is a named business leader with approval authority over a domain; the steward does the day-to-day work of maintaining definitions and monitoring quality; the custodian implements the technical storage, security, and movement of the data.

The owner is a named business leader with approval authority over a domain; the steward implements the technical storage and security of the data; the custodian maintains business definitions and monitors quality.
The custodian holds final approval authority over a domain, while the owner implements the technical database infrastructure.
Owner, steward, and custodian are three different names for exactly the same role, just used by different departments.
Only the custodian role requires any business context at all; owners and stewards are purely technical positions.
A data steward always outranks a data owner in any domain-level decision.
questions.explain: The owner holds approval authority at the business level; the steward does the recurring work of maintaining definitions and monitoring quality; the custodian implements the technical environment — storage, security, movement. They're three different jobs, usually held by three different kinds of people.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps the correct description of the owner, which makes it tempting — but it swaps the steward's and custodian's actual jobs with each other. The steward maintains business definitions and monitors quality, not technical storage; the custodian implements technical storage and security, not business definitions. That swap is the one meaningful detail that makes B wrong.

questions.prompt: Match each governance role to the question it answers, per this course.
right: Who decides what the rules are?
What does this data mean, and is it meeting the quality bar?
Where does this data physically live, and who implements the controls?
Anyone who uses data to do their job without holding owner, steward, or custodian responsibility for it
questions.explain: The owner decides the rules, the steward maintains meaning and quality, the custodian handles the physical/technical environment, and the consumer is everyone else who uses the data day to day without holding one of the three formal roles.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement below about governance councils and committees, per this course.
options: A governance committee typically draws from business, IT, security, legal, and compliance
The committee is usually where cross-domain disputes that owners can't resolve alone land
The committee's job includes formally empowering owners and stewards, making role assignments visible and legitimate
Every organization needs exactly four distinct governance layers, with no exceptions
A smaller organization can compress the council and committee into one group that meets monthly
questions.explain: A committee draws from multiple functions, handles cross-domain disputes, and formally empowers roles. It is NOT true that every organization needs exactly four layers — a smaller organization can run with just two, compressing the council and committee into one group, as long as some standing cross-functional forum exists above individual owners.

questions.prompt: A team builds a RACI matrix for a governance activity, and one row lists both the data owner and the governance committee as Accountable for the same task. Per this course, what's wrong with this row?
options: A task with more than one Accountable hasn't actually clarified responsibility — it has just written down the same ambiguity that caused the original problem
Nothing is wrong — a task can have as many Accountable roles as there are stakeholders involved
The row is fine as long as both parties are also marked Responsible for the same task
This is only a problem if the task also lists more than one Consulted role
questions.explain: A RACI matrix stops being useful the moment a single task has more than one A. Two people both Accountable for the same activity means responsibility hasn't actually been clarified — it's the exact ambiguity that caused the original problem, just written down instead of fixed.

questions.prompt: A governance program's executive sponsor has never attended a committee meeting, and governance work routinely loses out to other priorities with no pushback from the top. Per this course, what does this indicate?
options: Sponsorship has become a line on an org chart rather than an active role — a sign of sponsorship in name only
This is normal, sustained sponsorship, since a sponsor's job is only to approve the program once at launch
This indicates the organization has successfully reached the 'Optimized' maturity level
This indicates the governance committee has taken over the sponsor's role entirely, which is the intended outcome
questions.explain: A sponsor who's never attended a meeting and whose program routinely loses out to other priorities with no pushback is exactly the signal that sponsorship has quietly become sponsorship in name only — a line on an org chart rather than an active, ongoing role.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a living, governed reference that establishes one standard definition per business term, so different teams don't quietly mean different things by "active customer," is called a ________.
questions.explain: A business glossary defines business concepts, their relationships, and how each one maps to actual physical data — the living reference that prevents the same term from meaning five different things across five systems.

questions.prompt: A bank states: "All customer financial information is highly confidential and may only be accessed on a need-to-know basis." A companion document states: "All customer account numbers must be 10 digits, starting with two letters identifying the region." Per this course, which is the policy and which is the standard?
options: The confidentiality statement is the policy (what's required and why); the account-number format is the standard (the concrete, checkable rule that implements it)
The account-number format is the policy; the confidentiality statement is the standard
Both statements are policies — standards only ever apply to encryption algorithms, never to account formats
Both statements are standards — policies only ever apply to access control, never to confidentiality
questions.explain: A policy states what is required and why, staying implementation-agnostic — the confidentiality statement. A standard provides the concrete, checkable detail that implements it — the exact account-number format. Neither works well without the other.

questions.prompt: Put the six stages of the policy lifecycle in the correct order, per this course.
items: Drafting — the policy owner identifies the need and produces a first controlled version
Review — legal, compliance, IT, and the governance committee assess the draft
Approval — the authorized body approves, rejects, or sends the draft back for changes
Publication — the approved policy reaches the people expected to follow it
Review and revision — the policy is checked on a schedule or triggered early by a change
Retirement — the outdated policy is formally retired and removed from active circulation
questions.explain: A policy moves from drafting through review, approval, publication, ongoing review and revision, and eventually formal retirement. Retirement is the stage organizations handle worst — it's far easier to stop thinking about an old policy than to formally mark it retired.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement below about technical policy enforcement mechanisms, per this course.
options: Access control (RBAC/ABAC) that blocks unauthorized access automatically
Automated classification that tags sensitive data so a policy has something concrete to apply to
Real-time monitoring and alerts that flag a policy violation as it happens
Audit trails — an immutable log of who accessed or changed what
Training and acknowledgment, where people formally confirm they've read the rule
questions.explain: Access control, automated classification, monitoring/alerts, and audit trails are all technical enforcement mechanisms — they apply the rule automatically at the point data is touched. Training and acknowledgment is organizational enforcement, not technical: it depends on people remembering, not a system checking.

questions.prompt: Which statement below correctly describes the structural difference between GDPR's and CCPA's consent models, per this course?
options: GDPR generally defaults to opt-in consent before processing personal data; CCPA generally defaults to opt-out, where a business can collect data by default and the consumer must actively opt out of its sale or sharing.
GDPR generally defaults to opt-in consent before processing personal data; CCPA generally defaults to requiring the exact same opt-in consent, just enforced by a different regulator.

CCPA applies globally to any organization processing EU residents' data, while GDPR applies only to California residents, which is the exact reverse of each regulation's own real, documented jurisdictional scope today.
GDPR and CCPA both use an opt-out model, with no meaningful structural difference between them.
HIPAA, not GDPR, is the regulation that introduced the opt-in consent model this lesson describes.
GDPR's opt-in requirement was retired and replaced by an opt-out model in its most recent revision.
questions.explain: GDPR generally defaults to opt-in consent before processing personal data. CCPA/CPRA generally defaults to opt-out for the sale or sharing of personal information — a business can collect and process data by default, and it's the consumer's responsibility to actively opt out. This is the single structural fact the lesson says trips people up most.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps the correct description of GDPR's opt-in default, which is what makes it the closest wrong answer — but it claims CCPA requires 'the exact same opt-in consent.' The lesson's central point is exactly the opposite: CCPA defaults to opt-out, the structurally different mechanic from GDPR's opt-in, not a different regulator enforcing the same rule.

questions.prompt: Instead of a policy stating "only approved systems may read this table" and hoping every engineer remembers to check, a control is written as executable logic inside the data pipeline that automatically blocks an unapproved read attempt the moment it's tried. Per this course, what is this called?
options: Policy-as-code
Organizational enforcement
A governance council
A maturity assessment
questions.explain: Policy-as-code means writing governance rules as executable logic embedded directly into data pipelines, so the system itself checks and blocks a violation, rather than depending entirely on human memory to catch it after the fact.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the measured current state of whatever a pilot's objective is about, captured before anything changes so the "after" number actually means something, is called the pilot's ________.
questions.explain: A baseline is captured before a pilot starts, so the end-of-pilot result can actually be compared against something real — without it, a scale-or-stop decision has no evidence to work from.

questions.prompt: Select every one of the six readiness-assessment dimensions this course describes.
options: Current data practices
Executive sponsorship
Organizational structure
Existing policy and standards
Technology and tooling
Regulatory and risk pressure
Current stock price performance
Office floor-plan layout
questions.explain: The six real dimensions are current data practices, executive sponsorship, organizational structure, existing policy and standards, technology and tooling, and regulatory and risk pressure. Stock price performance and office layout aren't readiness dimensions this course describes at all.

questions.prompt: Match each component of a credible business case to its correct description, per this course.
left: Anticipated value and how you'll measure it
right: A real or representative anecdote a non-technical sponsor already recognizes, not an abstract metadata complaint
Typically a scoped pilot, not a company-wide program on day one
People (even part-time), tooling budget if needed, and executive sponsorship itself as a resource
Tied to something the audience already tracks, like reconciliation hours or compliance findings, not a vague claim like 'better data culture'
questions.explain: A credible business case states the problem in business terms, proposes a scoped solution, names real resources including sponsorship itself, and ties anticipated value to something the audience already tracks, rather than a vague, unmeasurable claim.

questions.prompt: A proposed pilot domain is high-value and high-pain, but it spans twelve systems and four business units, with no realistic way for a small team to finish anything in a 90-day window. Per this course, what's the actual problem with this pilot choice?
options: It fails the feasibility criterion — a domain this large is a program, not a pilot, which is the single most common way 'starting small' quietly turns into 'starting the same big thing, just called a pilot'
There is no problem — value and pain are the only two criteria that actually matter for choosing a pilot
The domain should be rejected only because it lacks executive sponsorship, not because of its size
Twelve systems is actually the ideal pilot size recommended by this course
questions.explain: A good pilot domain needs high value, high pain, AND high feasibility. A domain spanning twelve systems and four business units fails feasibility, no matter how high its value and pain scores are — which is exactly the trap that turns a pilot into a program wearing a pilot's name.

questions.prompt: Put the five phases of a governance roadmap in the correct order, per this course.
items: Discovery (Days 0-30) — confirm goals, stakeholders, and critical domains
Foundation (Days 31-60) — assign first owners and stewards, document first policies
Pilot (Days 61-90) — launch the governance workflow for one chosen domain
Expand (Months 3-6) — apply what worked in the pilot to two or three more domains
Scale (Months 6-12) — governance becomes business-as-usual through the standing operating model
questions.explain: The realistic phase structure runs discovery, foundation, pilot, expand, and scale — each phase needs its own named owner, defined output, and measurable milestone, not just a date on a timeline.

questions.prompt: At Meridian Fulfillment Co., the VP sponsor announces the customer-address pilot as "this is how we stop shipping to the wrong address" rather than "here's a new policy you have to follow." Per this course, why does this framing matter?
options: Framing governance as an enabler of something people already want, rather than a constraint being imposed on them, is what actually gets a willing audience for the exact same underlying program
It doesn't matter — this course states that framing has no measurable effect on how a message is received
This framing is only appropriate for an all-staff town hall, never for a small, targeted pilot like Meridian's
This framing is required specifically because customer address data is subject to HIPAA
questions.explain: The same program described as 'rules you now have to follow' versus 'the reason you'll stop shipping to the wrong address' is the same underlying work — but only the enabler framing gets a willing audience. This is exactly why Meridian's VP led with the business problem being solved, not the policy being imposed.
